pairs.b: archive:archive:memory_dropout_coadaptation: Don't Co-Adapt: A Bank-Swap Diagnostic for
pairs.prior_text:
archive:memory_dropout_coadaptation: Don't Co-Adapt: A Bank-Swap Diagnostic for Prompt Optimizers Coupled to Self-Editing Memory, and Which Fix Actually Survives Bank Turnover. When a reflective prompt optimizer evolves instructions while a retrieved experience memory is injected, it exploits the specific bank present at optimization time; because self-editing banks turn over in deployment, the resulting instruction is brittle and much of its measured gain does not survive a bank swap. The fragility is a property of the *optimization-time context distribution*, not of the deployment-time injection budget: randomizing that distribution during optimization (masking the injected memory block with probability p) should reduce the bank-dependence gap more than any deployment-side knob applied to an already co-adapted instruction, including reducing top-k at test time. The claim is not about dropout as a device: if shard resampling of the bank works equally well, the hypothesis survives and the instantiation changes; if deployment-time top-k tuning removes the gap just as well, the hypothesis is refuted and we say so. Agent stacks increasingly place an automatic prompt optimizer on top of a self-editing experience memory and optimize the prompt with memory injection switched on. We argue this is a train/deploy mismatch: the instruction is evolved against one particular bank, but banks are rewritten continuously as the agent accumulates and prunes experience, so any gain that depends on bank-specific content evaporates. Pilot measurements motivating this work show that prompt evolution's apparent gains were largely redistribution (as many items fixed as broken), that memory injection can be one-sidedly harmful, that injection *volume* rather than content was the causal lever for that harm, and that the two components fail on disjoint slices.

That last pilot finding sets up the sharpest version of our claim. If the fragility were just an injection-budget problem, it would be curable at deployment by lowering top-k on the new bank, with no re-optimization at all. We test that directly. We propose memory dropout — during optimization rollouts the injected memory block is masked with probability p, so the optimizer sees the bank as a random rather than fixed context — and evaluate three levels (p=0, standard practice; p=0.5; p=1, memory-free optimization) on a single primary task (multi-hop QA with a retrieval tool) with a single 7B open-weight agent model, four optimizer seeds per level, and 800 item-paired held-out questions under three deployment banks (own, swapped, none). The primary endpoint is accuracy under the swapped bank; the primary diagnostic is D_swap = acc(own bank) − acc(swapped bank). Running in the same grid: a length-matched neutral-block dropout arm (memory-specific vs. generic perturbation), a deployment-time top-k reduction arm applied to co-adapted instructions (the reviewer-named competing fix, and the one that could kill the method), a write-path-curated bank, bank-shard randomization, and full re-optimization as the engineering upper bound. Every fix is reported with its optimization cost in LLM calls. We pre-register decision rules under which the honest conclusion becomes "just lower k at deployment", "optimize memory-free", or "any context randomization works", and report all effects against a measured null-replicate noise floor. The study is 21 optimization runs and ~70k paired evaluation episodes on one 4×A100 node, with frontier API use confined to bank distillation, reflection, and judging (≤$200).

pairs.prior_text: arxiv:2603.21520: Automatic prompt optimization should be reformulated as continual experience accumulation: a dual memory of reusable strategy templates and structured error patterns, retrieved to compose prompts and refined by self-reflection, consistently outperforms representative prompt optimization baselines while substantially reducing optimization cost.

archive:memory_volume_amplifies_optimizer_curse: Does Retrieved Memory Inflate the Optimizer's Curse? Injection Budget as a Lever on Selection Bias in Agent Prompt Search. The headline claim is the coupling, not the curse. (i) **Mechanism:** injecting k retrieved experience items into a ReAct agent inflates the run-to-run variance of its validation score (E0), so a prompt optimizer searching over that agent selects more strongly on luck. (ii) **Consequence:** the fraction of a reflective prompt optimizer's reported validation gain that is pure selection bias — measured by a *null optimizer* whose proposal step is replaced by identity/judge-verified paraphrase — is strictly larger at k=7 than at k=0. If true, coupled memory+optimizer systems report gains that are increasingly selection artefact, which is a concrete explanation for why such gains do not replicate. (iii) **Remedy feasibility, measured not assumed:** the standard variance-reduction move, common random numbers over shared items and shared decoding seeds, may not survive interactivity because a changed prompt changes the action sequence; we decompose the cross-candidate correlation of per-item outcomes into item-sharing and seed-sharing components and report how much of each survives. (iv) **A separation we predict analytically and test:** empirical-Bayes shrinkage fixes the *reported number* but, under equal evaluation budgets, is rank-preserving and therefore cannot change *which* prompt is returned. The existence and rough size of the curse (claims (v) below) is treated as calibration/replication, not as novelty, because the track's own prior work already observed a null replicate matching the best real treatment. Automatic prompt optimizers return the candidate with the best validation score. When that score is noisy — as it is for LLM agents, where re-scoring one configuration on the same held-out set moves the metric by several points — the winner is selected partly for being lucky, and the reported gain is inflated. The mechanism is old (max-of-N extreme-value inflation; Dodge et al. 2019) and its qualitative presence in agent prompt search has already been observed. We therefore do not lead with it.

We lead with a coupling claim that follows from it. Prior controlled work in this line found that memory *injection volume* — how many retrieved experience items enter the context — is the causal lever for negative transfer. We argue volume is simultaneously a **variance** lever: more injected items lengthen and destabilize rollouts, inflating the score noise a prompt optimizer selects on. The prediction is sharp and testable: the fraction of an optimizer's reported validation gain that is pure selection bias is strictly larger at high injection budget than at zero. Coupled memory+optimizer systems would then report gains that are increasingly artefact, which is a mechanistic explanation for their non-replication.

We measure this with a **null optimizer**: the identical reflective loop with the proposal step replaced by identity or judge-verified semantics-preserving paraphrase, so any apparent improvement is selection bias accumulated over generations. Runs are paired by optimizer seed across k=0 and k=7, so the interaction is tested within-seed. A separate nested-ANOVA noise audit isolates the variance components (item sampling, decoding, injection) that the prediction rests on.

We then ask what can be done, and separate two answers usually conflated. Empirical-Bayes shrinkage corrects the *reported* number for free but, under equal evaluation budgets, is rank-preserving and cannot change *which* prompt is chosen. Changing the choice requires reducing the variance of candidate *differences* — common random numbers plus a paired acceptance test — and whether CRN survives in an interactive agent is precisely the objection to it. We answer it by measuring the residual cross-candidate correlation of per-item outcomes, split into item-sharing and seed-sharing components, and by comparing every selection rule (including an oracle ceiling and a random-choice floor) by Monte-Carlo resampling from a cached candidate × item × seed outcome tensor with ground truth on 1,200 held-out items — well powered at zero marginal rollout cost.

One task, one 7B model, 16 optimization runs, ~161k episodes, ~3 days on one node, <$200 API.

pairs.b: archive:archive:memory_vetoes_instruction_slot: The Instruction Slot Is Not Independent
pairs.prior_text:
archive:memory_vetoes_instruction_slot: The Instruction Slot Is Not Independent of the Memory Slot: Answer-Bearing Experience Suppresses Instruction Compliance Even Without Imitation, and Makes Optimized Prompts Bank-Specific. Prompt optimization assumes the instruction slot's contribution is separable from whatever occupies the demonstration slot. When that slot holds a live experience bank, the assumption fails in two measurable ways.

(1) **The veto.** A verification requirement ("do not answer until you have cited spans you retrieved this episode, and the citation must actually support the answer") is complied with at high rate with no memory and at equally high rate with token- and keyword-matched *answer-redacted* memory, and collapses under answer-bearing memory — same model, same instances, same semantic requirement. The trigger is the presence of a usable candidate answer in the retrieved item, not topical overlap (M2/M4), not context load (M4/M6), and not corruption of the memory: the harmful items are truthful records of tasks the agent previously solved correctly.

(2) **The dissociation from experience-following.** The compliance drop is present *even on episodes where the final answer does not match the retrieved memory* (non-echo subset). Output-imitation accounts (Xiong et al., ACL 2026) predict memory effects concentrate where outputs track memory; the veto predicts a compliance deficit where they do not. This is the discriminating measurement, and it costs no extra episodes.

(3) **The boundary, not a universal negative.** Within one run, the same GEPA/MIPROv2 search substantially repairs memory-echoed ungrounded answers (a content-selection failure evaluated at generation time) while barely touching insufficient-evidence errors (a termination failure decided against a candidate answer already in context). Optimizers are seeded with the target instruction, so the fix is provably in the search space.

(4) **The consequence.** Because the slots are entangled, instructions optimized with a bank in context lose most of their measured advantage when the bank is swapped for one built from a disjoint split, while instructions optimized without memory are bank-invariant. If so, prompt-optimization gains reported on memory-augmented agents are partly bank-specific and are mis-attributed to the prompt. Retrieved-experience memory frequently makes LLM agents worse, and the field's explanations are about memory quality: stale, misevolved, adversarial, conflicting, too long. We propose something sharper. The items that do the damage in our setting are *correct* — truthful records of tasks the agent previously solved — and the damage is not only that the agent copies them. It is that the agent stops obeying the instruction that would have caught the error.

The centerpiece is a compliance-by-memory-condition design. One semantic requirement — before answering, cite spans you retrieved in *this* episode, and the citation must support the answer — is measured per episode under three memory conditions: none, token- and keyword-matched answer-redacted memory, and answer-bearing memory. We predict compliance is high and statistically equivalent in the first two and collapses by ≥25 points in the third, in the same model on the same instances. This excludes the two standing rebuttals by construction rather than by argument: the model can obviously execute the instruction (it does so under two conditions), and an optimizer cannot have under-searched for a fix that we seed into its initial population.

One measurement decides whether this is a new claim or a restatement of experience-following (Xiong et al., ACL 2026, the closest prior work). Experience-following says memory effects are carried by output imitation. We restrict to episodes where the final answer does *not* match the retrieved memory and ask whether the compliance deficit survives. If it vanishes, their account subsumes ours and we report that.

Two results decide whether it matters. A within-run dissociation shows the same seeded GEPA and MIPROv2 searches substantially repair memory-echoed ungrounded answers while barely touching insufficient-evidence errors — so this is a rule with a boundary, not "hard constraints beat soft prompts." And a bank-swap arm tests whether instructions optimized with a bank in context are bank-entangled: if Δ(G1, Bank A) largely disappears under a bank built from a disjoint split while memory-free-optimized instructions are invariant, then prompt-optimization gains reported on memory-augmented agents are partly bank-specific, and every such report needs a bank-invariance control it currently does not run.

The program is staged so the first stage is a paper on its own: ~20.7k self-hosted episodes, ≤$240 API, one environment, instance-paired throughout with fix/break decompositions, null replicates, stated MDEs and pre-registered refutation conditions.

pairs.b: archive:archive:memory_or_instruction: Is Your Agent's Memory Just an Un-Optimized Promp
pairs.prior_text: archive:memory_or_instruction: Is Your Agent's Memory Just an Un-Optimized Prompt? Measuring the Residual Value of Retrieved Experience After Instruction Optimization. Published agentic-memory gains are measured against a hand-written instruction. We hypothesize that for procedural experience memory (ExpeL/ReasoningBank-style), most of that gain is *substitutable*: when a reflective prompt optimizer is given exactly the same training episodes that built the memory bank, the memory-vs-no-memory gap collapses by at least 60%, and a frozen instruction compiled offline from the whole bank — with no retrieval at inference — matches per-instance top-k retrieval at matched injected tokens. The residual, non-substitutable value of memory is concentrated in instances with genuinely instance-specific reusable content, which we verify with a deliberately non-compilable positive-control bank where substitution must fail. Agentic memory systems are evaluated by comparing an agent with a retrieved-experience bank against the same agent without one, holding a hand-written scaffold prompt fixed. Recent audits (MemDelta) show such comparisons are confounded by retrieval engineering; we identify a different and sharper confound. A memory bank distilled from training episodes and an instruction optimized on those *same* episodes are two containers for the same information, and the second is dramatically cheaper to serve — one prompt paid once, versus retrieved tokens paid every episode. We test substitution directly. Holding the agent, tools, retriever, training split and evaluation fixed, we build (i) an ExpeL-style bank with per-instance top-k retrieval, (ii) an instruction optimized by GEPA that never sees the bank, and (iii) a frozen instruction compiled offline from the whole bank with no retrieval at all, token-matched per instance to (i). The primary endpoint is the substitution ratio S: the fraction of memory's paired gain over no-memory at the hand-written instruction that disappears at the optimized instruction. We predict S ≥ 0.6 on a tool-augmented multi-hop QA agent and ≥ 0.7 on ALFWorld, and we predict the compiled static arm comes within 2 points of live retrieval. A deliberately non-compilable positive-control bank, seeded with near-duplicates of held-out instances, must show S < 0.25 — so a null on the main benchmarks is a finding rather than a power failure. The study is scoped to one primary environment (n=600 paired instances, 3 optimizer seeds), one replication environment, and ~30,000 evaluation episodes, with instance-paired McNemar tests, crossed random effects for optimizer seed, null replicates, and a stated minimum detectable effect.

pairs.b: archive:archive:memory_budget_confound: One Item Is the Budget: Token Volume, Not Memory
pairs.prior_text: archive:memory_budget_confound: One Item Is the Budget: Token Volume, Not Memory Content, Explains Both the Harm and the Apparent Gains of Agentic Memory Curation. In experience-memory agents, the value of injected retrieved experience saturates after roughly one item, while its cost grows with injected tokens regardless of relevance. Two consequences follow, both falsifiable: (i) length-matched decoy experience — same environment, wrong task — reproduces most of the harm of correctly retrieved experience at the same injection volume; (ii) published curation methods (reconstruction, self-organizing memory) lose most or all of their advantage over raw top-k retrieval once the raw baseline is given the same per-instance injected-token budget the curated output happens to consume. The practical corollary is that k=1 raw retrieval, tuned once, is competitive with curation at a fraction of the cost. Agentic memory systems retrieve distilled past experience and inject it into an LLM agent's context. A 2026 wave of papers documents that this often hurts, attributes the harm to memory content — staleness, conflict, the abstraction gap between stored experience and the current state — and proposes a content-side remedy: reconstruction, reorganization, pruning. Each remedy also changes how many tokens get injected, and none of the papers we could find matches its raw-retrieval baseline on that budget. We ask whether the harm, and the reported cure, are about content at all. A pilot observation motivates the doubt: for a fixed memory bank, cutting injection from seven retrieved items to three eliminated a significant harm (McNemar p<0.05, replicated) without changing a single item. We propose a decomposition that separates the *content* value of retrieved experience from the *load* cost of the tokens carrying it. Holding bank, retriever, scaffold, tools and decoding fixed, we vary relevance (correct retrieval vs. length-matched decoys drawn from the same environment but the wrong task, and from an unrelated environment), item count, and total injected tokens (equalized by padding and truncation), with a gold-trajectory oracle bounding content value from above and a cross-encoder reranker instantiating the content-selection alternative. We then apply the missing control to two reimplemented curation methods: give raw top-k the same per-instance injected-token budget the curated output consumes, and add a compression-only rewrite that strips situational grounding from reconstruction. The sharp prediction is that content value saturates after about one item while load cost is roughly linear in tokens and largely relevance-independent, so that tuned k=1 raw retrieval lands within 2 points of the best curation method. Analysis is fully paired, with null replicates that fix the noise floor and a pre-registered minimum detectable effect.

pairs.b: archive:archive:instruction_conditioned_complementarity: What Does the Prompt Already Sa
pairs.prior_text: archive:instruction_conditioned_complementarity: What Does the Prompt Already Say? Instruction-Conditioned Complementarity Decides When Retrieved Experience Helps, Hurts, or Just Costs Tokens. The marginal value of an injected memory item is relational: it is determined by the item's content relative to what the agent's *instruction* already states, not by the item's similarity to the query nor by its similarity to other retrieved items. Labeling each unit of guidance in a retrieved item against the instruction as REDUNDANT (already asserted), NOVEL (instruction silent) or CONFLICTING (instruction asserts something incompatible) yields a three-way decomposition that predicts per-instance outcomes: fixes track novel units, breaks track conflicting units, redundant units are pure token cost. Consequences we test: (a) the *same* memory bank flips from helpful to inert when the instruction is optimized, because its units become redundant; (b) surgically deleting only the redundant units preserves accuracy at ~half the injected tokens while a token-matched random deletion does not; (c) deleting novel units destroys the fixes; (d) a retrieval rule that scores candidates by instruction-conditional novel-unit yield per token beats similarity top-k and item-diversity MMR at matched budget. Agentic memory retrieves past experience by similarity to the query and injects it alongside a task instruction that a prompt optimizer is separately rewriting. Both texts carry guidance; nothing in either pipeline checks whether they carry the *same* guidance. We propose that an item's marginal value is relational — it depends on what the instruction already says — and that this single variable explains the fix/break/token-cost structure of memory injection that recent empirical work documents but does not predict. We decompose the instruction and each retrieved item into atomic guidance units and label every item unit against the instruction as redundant, novel, or conflicting, using an off-the-shelf NLI model as the primary instrument (LLM and human labels used for validation only). We test three things on one environment with one primary model. First, relationality: holding the bank, retriever and retrievals fixed, we run under a short hand-written instruction and under an optimizer-produced long instruction, and predict that the same items flip from mostly novel to substantially redundant and that memory's paired gain collapses accordingly. Second, causality: unit-level surgery at matched token budget — delete only the redundant units, delete a token-matched random subset, delete the novel units, or delete a subset chosen against a *decoy* instruction — so the taxonomy can be falsified without touching the retriever. Third, exploitation: a complementarity retrieval rule scoring candidates by instruction-conditional novel-unit yield per token, against similarity top-k, MMR item-diversity, and a cheap embedding-overlap proxy at matched injected-token budgets. All comparisons are instance-paired with McNemar tests, null replicates, and a stated 5-point minimum detectable effect at n=500. The whole program is ~27k agent episodes on one 4×A100 node and under $100 of API.

pairs.b: archive:archive:memory_induced_shortcutting: Memory Makes Agents Stop Looking: Premature
pairs.prior_text:
archive:memory_induced_shortcutting: Memory Makes Agents Stop Looking: Premature Termination of Evidence Gathering Mediates Memory Harm, and Instruction Optimization Cannot Repair It. When retrieved-experience memory breaks an otherwise-solvable task, the proximate cause is usually that the agent stopped gathering evidence early — it treats a past outcome as if it were evidence about the current instance and terminates after fewer tool calls — rather than that it executed a specific bad action recommended by memory. Three consequences follow and are tested: (i) memory items that carry an OUTCOME (a past answer or completed result) cause shortcutting, while token-matched process-only items do not; (ii) a content-free evidence floor enforced in the control flow (the agent may not answer until it has itself retrieved spans that support its answer) removes most of the harm while preserving the benefit, and helps the memory-augmented agent far more than the memory-free one; (iii) the repair belongs to the control flow and not the instruction slot — a GEPA-optimized instruction, searched with full reflective access to shortcutting failures, will not recover the floor's benefit. Claim (iii) is the division-of-labour claim: some agent pathologies are not addressable by prompt optimization at all. Retrieved-experience memory frequently makes LLM agents worse, and the field's explanations are about what is in the memory: it is stale, non-transferable, conflicting, or simply too long. We propose a procedural explanation instead. An agent working a multi-step task must decide when it has looked enough; a retrieved item about a similar past task supplies a plausible-looking answer, and the agent stops early, answering on evidence it never gathered. Under this account the harm is not that the agent follows bad advice but that it truncates its own search, and it is therefore repairable without touching memory content — but only by an intervention that lives in the control flow.

We test three things on one primary environment. First, mediation: on instances that memory breaks, do trajectories shorten, and does the memory-versus-no-memory break effect lose most of its coefficient once evidence-gathering depth and evidence sufficiency are entered? Second, a token-matched content decomposition: outcome-redacted items (procedure kept, past answer deleted) versus outcome-only items versus topically irrelevant decoys. The shortcutting account predicts redaction keeps most of the fixes and sheds most of the breaks, while decoys do not truncate at all. Third, and centrally, a ladder of repairs at three levels of the agent stack: a hand-written self-verification instruction, a GEPA-searched instruction optimized with reflective access to the shortcutting failures, and a content-free evidence floor enforced programmatically. The floor is applied to both the memory and memory-free arms, so the claim is an interaction and not "more search is good". Our sharp and risky prediction is that the two instruction-level repairs, including the searched one, recover less than a third of the floor's benefit: premature commitment is a control-flow property that the instruction slot cannot own. A perturbed-corpus probe, where the current answer deliberately differs from what a topically similar past episode implies, gives a positive control in which shortcutting must produce a specific identifiable wrong answer. All comparisons are instance-paired with fix/break decompositions, null replicates, and a stated minimum detectable effect, inside a budget of ~23k episodes and ~$120 of API spend.

pairs.b: archive:archive:memory_or_instruction: Is Your Agent's Memory Just an Un-Optimized Promp
pairs.prior_text: archive:memory_or_instruction: Is Your Agent's Memory Just an Un-Optimized Prompt? Measuring the Residual Value of Retrieved Experience After Instruction Optimization. Published agentic-memory gains are measured against a hand-written instruction. We hypothesize that for procedural experience memory (ExpeL/ReasoningBank-style), most of that gain is *substitutable*: when a reflective prompt optimizer is given exactly the same training episodes that built the memory bank, the memory-vs-no-memory gap collapses by at least 60%, and a frozen instruction compiled offline from the whole bank — with no retrieval at inference — matches per-instance top-k retrieval at matched injected tokens. The residual, non-substitutable value of memory is concentrated in instances with genuinely instance-specific reusable content, which we verify with a deliberately non-compilable positive-control bank where substitution must fail. Agentic memory systems are evaluated by comparing an agent with a retrieved-experience bank against the same agent without one, holding a hand-written scaffold prompt fixed. Recent audits (MemDelta) show such comparisons are confounded by retrieval engineering; we identify a different and sharper confound. A memory bank distilled from training episodes and an instruction optimized on those *same* episodes are two containers for the same information, and the second is dramatically cheaper to serve — one prompt paid once, versus retrieved tokens paid every episode. We test substitution directly. Holding the agent, tools, retriever, training split and evaluation fixed, we build (i) an ExpeL-style bank with per-instance top-k retrieval, (ii) an instruction optimized by GEPA that never sees the bank, and (iii) a frozen instruction compiled offline from the whole bank with no retrieval at all, token-matched per instance to (i). The primary endpoint is the substitution ratio S: the fraction of memory's paired gain over no-memory at the hand-written instruction that disappears at the optimized instruction. We predict S ≥ 0.6 on a tool-augmented multi-hop QA agent and ≥ 0.7 on ALFWorld, and we predict the compiled static arm comes within 2 points of live retrieval. A deliberately non-compilable positive-control bank, seeded with near-duplicates of held-out instances, must show S < 0.25 — so a null on the main benchmarks is a finding rather than a power failure. The study is scoped to one primary environment (n=600 paired instances, 3 optimizer seeds), one replication environment, and ~30,000 evaluation episodes, with instance-paired McNemar tests, crossed random effects for optimizer seed, null replicates, and a stated minimum detectable effect.

archive:commit_then_consult_slot_discipline: Anchoring, Not Overload: Commitment Order Explains Why Optimized Instructions and Agent Experience Memory Fight Each Other. Harm from injected agent memory is a *slot violation resolved by order*: retrieved experience that is directive (imperative procedural content) occupies the demonstration slot but functions as an instruction, and because it arrives before the agent has committed to anything, it overrides plans the agent would otherwise have executed correctly. Three consequences, all testable at fixed injected-token count. (1) Ordering fix: commit-then-consult — draft and log a plan/answer with no memory, then revise against your own logged draft plus the *identical* retrieved items — sharply cuts breaks while preserving fixes, which the injection-volume account predicts it cannot. (2) Slot fix: routing the directive content out of the memory slot into the optimizer-owned instruction slot, where GEPA vets it against a training signal, neutralizes the same harm, and the two fixes are redundant rather than additive because they target one mechanism. (3) The risky coupling prediction: prompt optimization and memory are *anti-synergistic under memory-first ordering* — a GEPA-optimized instruction gives the agent a stronger correct prior to abandon, so memory harm gets **larger**, not smaller, after instruction optimization, and the anti-synergy disappears under commit-then-consult. Agentic memory systems retrieve distilled past experience and place it in the agent's context before it acts. A 2026 wave of results shows this frequently hurts, and every proposed remedy edits the memory: prune it, reconstruct it, restructure retrieval, or retrieve less. We propose that a large share of the harm is neither content nor volume but **order**. Retrieved experience that reads as a directive ("always search the entity page first") is instruction-shaped content sitting in the demonstration slot; presented before the agent has committed to anything, it functions as a command rather than as evidence, and the agent abandons plans it would have executed correctly. A pilot is consistent with this: injecting a retrieved bank fixed zero items and broke six to seven — a one-sided signature noise does not produce.

We test the anchoring account with an intervention that changes only ordering: **commit-then-consult**, where the agent first produces and logs a plan/answer with no memory, then sees its own logged draft alongside the *identical* retrieved items. The deciding pass contains the same memory tokens as the standard agent, so the volume account predicts no benefit. We then push the account into the space the track cares about: if the harm is instruction-shaped content in the wrong slot, then (i) routing directives into the optimizer-owned instruction slot should fix it the same way, redundantly rather than additively, and (ii) **GEPA-optimized instructions should make memory-first injection more harmful, not less**, because a better instruction is a better prior to abandon. That anti-synergy, and its disappearance under commit-then-consult, is our sharpest and riskiest prediction. Fully paired McNemar designs, null replicates, a stated minimum detectable effect, a directly implemented single-pass reconciliation baseline, a content-rewriting baseline, and a smaller-k baseline that could each refute us.

pairs.b: archive:archive:memory_budget_confound: One Item Is the Budget: Token Volume, Not Memory
pairs.prior_text: archive:memory_budget_confound: One Item Is the Budget: Token Volume, Not Memory Content, Explains Both the Harm and the Apparent Gains of Agentic Memory Curation. In experience-memory agents, the value of injected retrieved experience saturates after roughly one item, while its cost grows with injected tokens regardless of relevance. Two consequences follow, both falsifiable: (i) length-matched decoy experience — same environment, wrong task — reproduces most of the harm of correctly retrieved experience at the same injection volume; (ii) published curation methods (reconstruction, self-organizing memory) lose most or all of their advantage over raw top-k retrieval once the raw baseline is given the same per-instance injected-token budget the curated output happens to consume. The practical corollary is that k=1 raw retrieval, tuned once, is competitive with curation at a fraction of the cost. Agentic memory systems retrieve distilled past experience and inject it into an LLM agent's context. A 2026 wave of papers documents that this often hurts, attributes the harm to memory content — staleness, conflict, the abstraction gap between stored experience and the current state — and proposes a content-side remedy: reconstruction, reorganization, pruning. Each remedy also changes how many tokens get injected, and none of the papers we could find matches its raw-retrieval baseline on that budget. We ask whether the harm, and the reported cure, are about content at all. A pilot observation motivates the doubt: for a fixed memory bank, cutting injection from seven retrieved items to three eliminated a significant harm (McNemar p<0.05, replicated) without changing a single item. We propose a decomposition that separates the *content* value of retrieved experience from the *load* cost of the tokens carrying it. Holding bank, retriever, scaffold, tools and decoding fixed, we vary relevance (correct retrieval vs. length-matched decoys drawn from the same environment but the wrong task, and from an unrelated environment), item count, and total injected tokens (equalized by padding and truncation), with a gold-trajectory oracle bounding content value from above and a cross-encoder reranker instantiating the content-selection alternative. We then apply the missing control to two reimplemented curation methods: give raw top-k the same per-instance injected-token budget the curated output consumes, and add a compression-only rewrite that strips situational grounding from reconstruction. The sharp prediction is that content value saturates after about one item while load cost is roughly linear in tokens and largely relevance-independent, so that tuned k=1 raw retrieval lands within 2 points of the best curation method. Analysis is fully paired, with null replicates that fix the noise floor and a pre-registered minimum detectable effect.

pairs.b: archive:archive:collection_policy_coupling_collapse: Rich Get Richer, Twice: The Collect
pairs.prior_text: archive:collection_policy_coupling_collapse: Rich Get Richer, Twice: The Collection Policy — Not Content Quality — Drives Diversity Collapse When Self-Editing Memory and Prompt Optimization Share the Same Episodes. Degradation in self-evolving agents is caused by the *collection policy*: the episodes that generate new memory items (and new instructions) are themselves executed while conditioned on the current memory, so retrieved items reproduce themselves and the bank's effective support contracts. Content quality is not the lever. Two sharp predictions follow. (1) At matched content volume, growth rate, task draws and write path, a bank grown from memory-OFF episodes preserves retrievable diversity and tail-task accuracy, while the standard coupled loop contracts and accrues a tail-concentrated, break-dominated harm — and content-side write gates (verification/self-consistency) do *not* fix it. (2) Coupling a second self-editing artifact to the same retrieval-conditioned episodes compounds the harm: a reflective prompt optimizer evolved against a contracting bank writes instructions that presuppose the contracted support, so the evolved instruction *transfers* the damage even when paired with a diverse bank. A 50% mixing rate of decoupled collection episodes is the one-line fix. Self-evolving agents write distillations of their own episodes into a memory bank and retrieve from it on later episodes; a 2026 wave of results shows this degrades performance and attributes the degradation to a property of the written content — hallucinated, spurious, self-confirming, non-transferable — so every proposed remedy is a write-time content filter. We argue the causal variable is the collection policy, not the content. Because episodes are executed while conditioned on retrieved items, the distillations written back are downstream of what was retrieved; retrieval frequency is self-reinforcing and the bank's effective support contracts. We test this with a decoupling design: banks grown over identical cycles from identical task draws with an identical write path and identical write counts, differing only in whether the collecting episodes ran with memory in context. We then make the track's coupling question first-class by crossing that factor with a reflective prompt optimizer, giving a 2×2 over which self-editing channel is coupled to the retrieval-conditioned episodes, and we add an instruction/bank transplant test: if the optimizer's instruction has co-adapted to a contracted support, it should carry the harm to a healthy bank. We measure bank contraction (embedding effective rank, retrieval-count Gini, cluster coverage) against a size-matched random-bank null, and split downstream accuracy into head and tail task clusters with fix/break decompositions. Competing baselines are a correctness-gated write path, a diversity-gated write path, and coupled-but-random retrieval, each of which would win if the mechanism is content quality, coverage-at-write-time, or memory presence per se. A null on coupled-versus-decoupled refutes us and vindicates the content-side account; a coupled arm that beats decoupled on head accuracy with no tail deficit vindicates the "loop as efficiency mechanism" account of CoEvo-Mem. The whole design is one environment, three growth cycles, ~35k episodes on a single 4×A100 node and under $150 of API spend.

archive:memory_volume_amplifies_optimizer_curse: Does Retrieved Memory Inflate the Optimizer's Curse? Injection Budget as a Lever on Selection Bias in Agent Prompt Search. The headline claim is the coupling, not the curse. (i) **Mechanism:** injecting k retrieved experience items into a ReAct agent inflates the run-to-run variance of its validation score (E0), so a prompt optimizer searching over that agent selects more strongly on luck. (ii) **Consequence:** the fraction of a reflective prompt optimizer's reported validation gain that is pure selection bias — measured by a *null optimizer* whose proposal step is replaced by identity/judge-verified paraphrase — is strictly larger at k=7 than at k=0. If true, coupled memory+optimizer systems report gains that are increasingly selection artefact, which is a concrete explanation for why such gains do not replicate. (iii) **Remedy feasibility, measured not assumed:** the standard variance-reduction move, common random numbers over shared items and shared decoding seeds, may not survive interactivity because a changed prompt changes the action sequence; we decompose the cross-candidate correlation of per-item outcomes into item-sharing and seed-sharing components and report how much of each survives. (iv) **A separation we predict analytically and test:** empirical-Bayes shrinkage fixes the *reported number* but, under equal evaluation budgets, is rank-preserving and therefore cannot change *which* prompt is returned. The existence and rough size of the curse (claims (v) below) is treated as calibration/replication, not as novelty, because the track's own prior work already observed a null replicate matching the best real treatment. Automatic prompt optimizers return the candidate with the best validation score. When that score is noisy — as it is for LLM agents, where re-scoring one configuration on the same held-out set moves the metric by several points — the winner is selected partly for being lucky, and the reported gain is inflated. The mechanism is old (max-of-N extreme-value inflation; Dodge et al. 2019) and its qualitative presence in agent prompt search has already been observed. We therefore do not lead with it.

We lead with a coupling claim that follows from it. Prior controlled work in this line found that memory *injection volume* — how many retrieved experience items enter the context — is the causal lever for negative transfer. We argue volume is simultaneously a **variance** lever: more injected items lengthen and destabilize rollouts, inflating the score noise a prompt optimizer selects on. The prediction is sharp and testable: the fraction of an optimizer's reported validation gain that is pure selection bias is strictly larger at high injection budget than at zero. Coupled memory+optimizer systems would then report gains that are increasingly artefact, which is a mechanistic explanation for their non-replication.

We measure this with a **null optimizer**: the identical reflective loop with the proposal step replaced by identity or judge-verified semantics-preserving paraphrase, so any apparent improvement is selection bias accumulated over generations. Runs are paired by optimizer seed across k=0 and k=7, so the interaction is tested within-seed. A separate nested-ANOVA noise audit isolates the variance components (item sampling, decoding, injection) that the prediction rests on.

We then ask what can be done, and separate two answers usually conflated. Empirical-Bayes shrinkage corrects the *reported* number for free but, under equal evaluation budgets, is rank-preserving and cannot change *which* prompt is chosen. Changing the choice requires reducing the variance of candidate *differences* — common random numbers plus a paired acceptance test — and whether CRN survives in an interactive agent is precisely the objection to it. We answer it by measuring the residual cross-candidate correlation of per-item outcomes, split into item-sharing and seed-sharing components, and by comparing every selection rule (including an oracle ceiling and a random-choice floor) by Monte-Carlo resampling from a cached candidate × item × seed outcome tensor with ground truth on 1,200 held-out items — well powered at zero marginal rollout cost.

One task, one 7B model, 16 optimization runs, ~161k episodes, ~3 days on one node, <$200 API.
